Part I develops the substantive intellectual intersection between economics and computer science. Its central premise is that many markets and institutions are now **designed, implemented, and mediated computationally**, while algorithms themselves operate in environments populated by strategic agents.

The first two modules build computational literacy for economists. The remainder develops the economic and computational analysis of strategic interaction, information, mechanisms, markets, networks, collective choice, learning, platforms, and digital institutions.

## Standard structure of a Part I module

Each module will eventually combine the economic question, formal model, computational formulation, algorithms and complexity, core courses and video lectures, seminal papers, cases and institutions, datasets, data labs, replications, implementation exercises, and research-frontier extensions.
:::

## Part I outcome

At the end of Part I, an economist should be comfortable formulating problems algorithmically and collaborating with computer scientists, while a computer scientist should have a rigorous economic framework for incentives, institutions, markets, and strategic behaviour.
